div.head: Chapter 24
div.p: As regards the second part of the conclusion — namely, that they are bound to make restitution, etc. — it is likewise proved by reasons and authorities. The first, because since restitution is to restore another to the state he was in when he possessed what was his and it was taken from him — that is to say, to the possession and lordship of that thing — which is nothing other than to preserve the equality of commutative justice that consists in a certain equality. And so restitution means to return or compensate a thing to its owner, which was unjustly taken from him, so that the equality may be repaired; because otherwise justice would not be preserved. And since to do and preserve justice is necessary, without the preservation of which it is impossible to be saved, from this it follows that the restitution of what was wrongly and unjustly taken and usurped is necessary for the salvation of each person, and without it it is impossible to be saved.

Now since those hundred and seventy men unjustly, with injurious violence, usurped that great principality, kingdoms and lordships of that King Atahualpa and of his heirs and of the other lords, their honors and royal dignities, the great treasures he gave for his ransom, and the immense quantities of gold and silver and precious stones that afterwards — his own and those of his vassals and of many other great lords and peoples — they robbed, with other irreparable wrongs and all with most grave and incomparable evils and harms: it follows that in order to restore and compensate them in their original state, which is to do and preserve justice, they are obliged to restore everything they robbed and the harms they did.

The second reason: each person is obliged to leave and abandon the mortal sin he committed, not to remain in it for even a single moment, because otherwise it is impossible to be saved, according to that passage of Ecclesiasticus 21: "Flee from sin as from the face of a serpent." For not only does he sin mortally who steals or robs another's property against the will of its owner, or in any other way harms his neighbor in that act and deed of usurping or causing harm, but also in retaining it against the will of its owner for even a single moment he holds it, he commits injury and causes harm to his neighbor against justice; therefore he sins mortally. The reason why the one who usurps another's property commits injury and injustice against the owner, and consequently commits sin, is that that act of theft or usurpation is done against the will of the owner. Therefore, if that usurpation and retention of another's property continues after that act against the will of the owner, injury and harm are always being done to him; therefore the sin always continues; therefore, in order to abandon mortal sin, restitution of what was stolen and robbed is necessary. And so, to restore what was wrongly acquired and robbed is nothing other than to cease from sin; and what has been said is confirmed, because whoever holds another's property is constrained to restore it by negative precept: Romans 13: "Owe nothing to anyone," et Leviticus 19. On this see Saint Thomas, 2.2 q. 62 a. final; et 4 Sent., dist. 15 q. 1 a. 5 qc. 1. Since it is the case that those who committed so many robberies and harms against so many thousands of persons of high and generous condition and diverse qualities are bound to restore and satisfy everything they robbed and damaged, and if they do not it is impossible for them to be saved.

The third: everything that is of divine precept a man must fulfill if he is to be saved, according to that passage of Matthew 19: "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments." Now the restitution of stolen things is of divine precept, Exodus 20: "You shall not steal." By which prohibition every illicit usurpation and harm to one's neighbor is generally prohibited, as appears from 14, q. 6, c. penale; and Saint Thomas, 2.2 q. 122 a. 6 ad 2. And in retaining another's property against the will of the owner, injury and harm are always being done, as has been proved; therefore, if restitution of what was stolen — as those men robbed and so greatly wronged their neighbors — is not made, they cannot be saved.

The fourth: whoever has the determined will to steal, there immediately arises from this an obligation and liability to eternal damnation, even if afterwards that will is interrupted by its contrary, unless he satisfies God through penance. So likewise in our present matter, no one, once he has incurred the obligation to restore something he has usurped, is released from it unless he restores what was robbed, or satisfies for the damages, losses, and injuries that were given or caused to another, as appears from the said chapter si culpa tua, De injuria et damno dato.

The fifth: let that sentence of Holy Scripture suffice, Leviticus 19: "The wages of your hired servant shall not remain with you until morning." Which authority, according to Thomas, is to be understood in all other restitutions, because the reason appears to be the same in all of them. Given that in the case of those tyrants of whom we speak, and others like them, who with such great injuries and so irreparable harms to their neighbors robbed and usurped things of such immense values and estimations, there must apply and run against them another reason more grave and binding to restore and satisfy with greater care all that is in their power, for they are already incapacitated by the greatness of the things robbed and the gravity of the harms they caused; for not even the kings of Spain, if they wished to satisfy for them by selling all their kingdoms — if they could be sold and a buyer were found — would it suffice to discharge and release them.

But because they have been and are very heedless of restoring or satisfying while yet alive, we can conclude that they are constantly in mortal sin, and those of them who are still living are in the state of eternal damnation, and those already dead are in hell, and thus it is impossible for them to be saved. This is proved by that passage of Saint Augustine, 14, q. 6, cap. si res, where he says: "If the thing on account of which one has sinned can be restored and is not restored, penance is not done but only simulated. And the sin is not forgiven unless what was taken away is restored." This is supported by the chapter falsas, De penitentia, Dist. 5 et in d. c. si culpa. Another part of the conclusion states that those hundred and seventy men are obliged to restore all the robberies and harms done by the Spaniards who came to those kingdoms afterwards and multiplied: which are to have despoiled many great lords of their honors and dignities and of their vassals and riches, and to have placed the peoples in the servitude of the repartimiento where they were harassed and oppressed, and the deaths and diminishment of infinite peoples: this is proved: because as regards both the sin and the restitution, the one is liable who gives occasion and opens the first gate to the sins and harms that neighbors receive, according to the rule of Christ, Matthew 18: "It is necessary that scandals come; but woe to the man through whom the scandal comes!" For "whoever gives cause or occasion for harm is held to have caused the harm," as in cap. Egressus, et in cap. si culpa, De injuria et damno dato, just as if certain persons were to do some injury or harm to some prince, who in order to avenge it were to make war upon an entire kingdom: for all the harms and deaths and robberies that kingdom would suffer, those persons would be liable. Argument, 23, q. 2, c. Dominus noster; and in the said cap. si culpa it says thus: "If through your fault the damage was caused or the injury inflicted, or you perhaps gave aid to those inflicting it, or this came about through your incompetence or negligence: by law you are bound to satisfy for it, nor does ignorance excuse you, if you ought to have known that an injury or loss could reasonably result from your act." Thus far there. Much pertinent to this is the chapter Hi quoscumque and the chapter placuit, the 29th, 1, q. 113: "For it makes no difference whether one kills, or gives the cause or occasion of death." ff. Ad legem Corneliam, De siccariis. From this comes what Saint Jerome says: that the punishments of Arius are not yet determined, because the number of those who are to be lost through that heresy has not yet come to an end. All of the foregoing is confirmed by ff., Ad legem Aquiliam, L. aquil l. qui occidit. §. in hac et ff., Si quadrupes pauperiem fecisse, L. 1, §. sed et si instigatu; ex ff. Ad legem Aquiliam, L. si servus, §. penúlt. et ff. De servo corrupto, §. Neratius. §. i.
